facts.fact_text: On 21 September 2015 the applicant, together with Ms S., notified the Syktyvkar Town Administration of their intention to hold a 'picket' (пикетирование) on 25 September 2015 from 5 to 6 p.m.
The 'picket' notified on 21 September 2015 was intended to be held at the crossroads of Lenin and Kommunisticheskaya streets behind the Lenin monument in Syktyvkar.
The 'picket' notified on 21 September 2015 was expected to be attended by fifty people.
The stated aim of the 'picket' notified on 21 September 2015 was to 'discuss the arrest of the Komi Republic government'.

In his Internet blog post of 21 September 2015, the applicant stated that the aim of the 'picket' was to let people express their thoughts about the arrests of members of the Komi Republic government.
In his Internet blog post of 21 September 2015, the applicant stated that any opinions — from approval to criticism of the arrests — were welcome at the 'picket'.

In his Internet blog post of 21 September 2015, the applicant stated that if the town administration proposed to hold the 'picket' on the outskirts of the town, a 'people's assembly' (народный сход), which did not require prior notification, would be held at the same location behind the Lenin monument.
In his Internet blog post of 22 September 2015, the applicant stated that a 'people's assembly' would be held instead at the same location and time as the originally planned 'picket'.
In his Internet blog post of 22 September 2015, the applicant explained that a 'people's assembly' was an assembly of people who gathered to discuss without there being any organisers.
In his Internet blog post of 22 September 2015, the applicant explained that unlike a 'picket', it was not possible to use placards during a 'people's assembly'.
At about 7 p.m. on 25 September 2015 about fifty people gathered near the Lenin monument in Syktyvkar.
The 'people's assembly' on 25 September 2015 near the Lenin monument went peacefully and without any disturbance.
On 21 September 2015 the Syktyvkar Town Administration refused to approve the venue chosen by the applicant for the 'picket'.

The Syktyvkar Town Administration's refusal of 21 September 2015 pointed out that Komi Republic regional law no. 91-RZ of 20 November 2012 [sic] prohibited the holding of public events in Stefanovskaya Square.
The Syktyvkar Town Administration proposed that the 'picket' be held at one of the special locations for public events designated by the Komi Republic government.
The applicant received the Syktyvkar Town Administration's decision of 21 September 2015 on 22 September 2015.
On 24 September 2015 the applicant's VKontakte account was blocked by the VKontakte administrator.
The applicant's VKontakte account was blocked on 24 September 2015 following an order by the Federal Service for Supervision of Communications, Information Technology and Mass Media.
The applicant's VKontakte account was blocked on 24 September 2015 following an order by a deputy Prosecutor General of the Russian Federation.

The deputy Prosecutor General found that the applicant's VKontakte post of 23 September 2015, which was publicly accessible, contained information about a 'picket' to be held on 25 September 2015 at the crossroads of Lenin and Kommunisticheskaya streets.

The deputy Prosecutor General found that the Syktyvkar Town Administration had refused to allow the 'picket' because it was prohibited to hold public events at the crossroads of Lenin and Kommunisticheskaya streets.

The deputy Prosecutor General found that the applicant's VKontakte post of 23 September 2015 amounted to campaigning for participation in an unlawful public event in breach of section 10 paragraph 1 of the Public Events Act.

The applicant's VKontakte account was blocked pursuant to section 15.3(1) of Law no. 149-FZ of 27 July 2006 on Information, Information Technologies and Protection of Information (the Information Act).

On 25 September 2015 the administrator of the Internet site that hosted the applicant's blog informed the applicant by email that access to the three blog entries (published on 21 September 2015, 22 September 2015, and 25 September 2015) had been restricted.
Access to the three blog entries was restricted on the order of the Prosecutor General's office.

The Prosecutor General's office ordered the restriction of access to the three blog entries because they had been found to contain calls to participate in public events held in breach of the established procedure.

In his appeal, the applicant submitted that the Syktyvkar Town Administration's decree no. 9/3483 of 4 September 2013, which allegedly prohibited public events at the crossroads of Lenin and Kommunisticheskaya streets, had never been published and was therefore not accessible to the public.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events in Stefanovskaya Square in the town of Syktyvkar.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events at railway stations, bus stations, markets, airports, educational institutions, buildings of educational institutions, religious buildings and areas within a radius of fifty metres of the entrance to those facilities.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events at children's playgrounds, locations designated by the municipal authorities for children's recreation and activities, pedestrian pavements, bus stops, and public parking areas.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events at buildings in a state of disrepair and areas within a radius of fifty metres of the entrance to such buildings.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events at buildings under construction, reconstruction or repair and areas within a radius of fifty metres of the entrance to such buildings.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic prohibits the holding of public events at buildings occupied by the regional authorities of the Komi Republic, Komi Republic branches of the federal authorities, the municipal authorities of the Komi Republic, state institutions in the Komi Republic and areas within a radius of fifty metres of the entrance to those buildings.

Section 5 of Komi Republic Law no. 91-RZ of 29 November 2012 on the Holding of Public Events in the Komi Republic provides that the listed prohibitions apply in addition to the locations where the holding of public events is prohibited pursuant to section 8 paragraph 2 of the Federal Public Events Act.

Syktyvkar Town Administration's decree no. 9/3483 of 4 September 2013 described the perimeter of the zone in the immediate vicinity of the Constitutional Court of the Komi Republic where the holding of public events was prohibited.

The perimeter described in Syktyvkar Town Administration's decree no. 9/3483 of 4 September 2013 comprised the entire Stefanovskaya Square and the adjacent streets, including the area at the crossroads of Lenin and Kommunisticheskaya streets.

Section 15.3(1) of Law no. 149-FZ of 27 July 2006 on Information, Information Technologies and Protection of Information (the Information Act), as in force at the material time, provided that if information disseminated through telecommunication networks, including the Internet, containing calls for mass disorder, extremist activities or participation in mass (public) events held in breach of the established procedure has been discovered, the Prosecutor General of the Russian Federation or his deputies shall order the federal law-enforcement authority supervising the mass media, mass communications and information technologies to take measures to restrict access to information media distributing that information.

Section 15.3(2) of the Information Act, as in force at the material time, provided that on the basis of the order mentioned in subsection 1, the federal law-enforcement authority supervising the mass media, mass communications and information technologies shall immediately order service providers to take measures to restrict access to the information medium or to the information published on it containing calls for mass disorder, extremist activities or participation in mass (public) events held in breach of the established procedure, mentioning the domain name, network address and URL of the webpage permitting identification of the information.

Section 15.3(2) of the Information Act, as in force at the material time, provided that the federal law-enforcement authority supervising the mass media, mass communications and information technologies shall identify the host service provider or person hosting the information medium on a telecommunication network such as the Internet or providing services to the owner of the website containing calls for mass disorder, extremist activities or participation in mass (public) events held in breach of the established procedure.

Section 15.3(2) of the Information Act, as in force at the material time, provided that the federal law-enforcement authority supervising the mass media, mass communications and information technologies shall send to the host service provider an electronic notification in Russian and English about a breach of the information distribution rules, mentioning the domain name, network address, and URL of the webpage permitting identification of the information, and an order to delete the information.

Section 15.3(2) of the Information Act, as in force at the material time, provided that the federal law-enforcement authority supervising the mass media, mass communications and information technologies shall record in a special electronic register the date and time when the notification was sent to the host service provider.

Section 15.3(3) of the Information Act, as in force at the material time, provided that upon receipt of the order to take measures to restrict access, the communications service provider permitting access to the Internet telecommunications network must immediately restrict access to the information medium or to information published thereon and containing calls for mass disorder, extremist activities or participation in mass (public) events held in breach of the established procedure.

Section 15.3(4) of the Information Act, as in force at the material time, provided that within twenty-four hours of receiving the notification, the host service provider must inform the owner of the information resource about the notification and that it is necessary to immediately delete the information containing calls for mass disorder, extremist activities or participation in mass (public) events held in breach of the established procedure.

Section 15.3(5) of the Information Act, as in force at the material time, provided that if the owner of the information medium has deleted the information containing calls for mass disorder, extremist activities or participation in mass (public) events held in breach of the established procedure, he must send a notification to the federal law-enforcement authority supervising the mass media, mass communications and information technologies, and such notification may be sent electronically.

Section 15.3(6) of the Information Act, as in force at the material time, provided that upon receipt of the notification that the information has been deleted, and after verifying its authenticity, the federal law-enforcement authority supervising the mass media, mass communications and information technologies must immediately send a notification to the communications service provider that it may reopen access to the information medium.

Section 15.3(7) of the Information Act, as in force at the material time, provided that upon receipt of the notification mentioned in subsection 6, the communications service provider shall immediately reopen access to the information medium.

The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic held in its judgment of 28 January 2016 that the Syktyvkar Town Administration's proposal to change the location of the public event chosen by the organisers had been substantiated, well reasoned and justified by the necessity to respect the balance of interests of the parties and to ensure public safety.

The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic held in its judgment of 28 January 2016 that there were objective and sufficient reasons for the proposal to change the location of the public event with the aim of ensuring a balance between the rights of the organisers and those of third persons.

The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic held in its judgment of 28 January 2016 that the Syktyvkar Town Administration's contested decision was in accordance with the Public Events Act, was made within the municipal authorities' powers and was in the interests of ensuring public order, with the aim of preventing disorder, protecting health and morality, and safeguarding the rights and freedoms of others.

The Syktyvkar Town Court held in its judgment of 5 April 2016 that the restriction on access to the applicant's information had a basis in law and pursued the aim of preventing breaches of law in the sphere of distribution of information.
The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic held on 14 December 2016 that calls for participation in public events held in breach of the established procedure were incompatible with public order.

The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic held on 14 December 2016 that the restriction on access to information containing calls for participation in public events held in breach of the established procedure pursued the aim of preventing more serious violations of public order.

The Syktyvkar Town Court held in its judgment of 18 November 2015 that the applicant's argument that the event would lose its purpose if held at the locations proposed by the Syktyvkar Town Administration was unsubstantiated.

The Syktyvkar Town Court noted in its judgment of 18 November 2015 that Decree no. 598 of 25 December 2012 by the Komi Republic Government designated special locations for holding public events in Syktyvkar, having ensured that they were in keeping with the aims of public events and accessible by public transport, permitted the organisers of and participants in public events to use public utility facilities, respected sanitary norms and rules, and guaranteed the safety of the organisers of and participants in public events.

The Syktyvkar Town Court noted in its judgment of 18 November 2015 that the Syktyvkar Town Administration's decision of 21 September 2015 mentioned the special locations designated by Decree no. 598 of 25 December 2012, de facto proposing them as an alternative to the location chosen by the applicant.

The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic held in its judgment of 28 January 2016 that the Syktyvkar Town Administration's proposal to change the location of the public event chosen by the organisers had been substantiated, well reasoned and justified by the necessity to respect the balance of interests of the parties and to ensure public safety.

The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic held in its judgment of 28 January 2016 that the applicant's argument that it was impossible to hold the event was hypothetical and did not refer to any valid reasons explaining why the locations proposed by the Syktyvkar Town Administration were incompatible with the public event's purposes.

The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic held in its judgment of 28 January 2016 that there were objective and sufficient reasons for the proposal to change the location of the public event with the aim of ensuring a balance between the rights of the organisers and those of third persons.

The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic held in its judgment of 28 January 2016 that the Syktyvkar Town Administration fulfilled its statutory obligation to propose an alternative location for the public event that was compatible with its purposes.

The Supreme Court of the Komi Republic held in its judgment of 28 January 2016 that the locations proposed by the Syktyvkar Town Administration were an adequate alternative to the chosen location and were in keeping with its purposes.
In his cassation appeal, the applicant added that public events were regularly held at the crossroads of Lenin and Kommunisticheskaya streets.

The Syktyvkar Town Court held in its judgment of 5 April 2016 that the applicant's freedom of expression was not restricted, because access was blocked to information distributed in breach of the law, rather than in connection with the contents of the applicant's statements about the aims of the notified public event.

The Syktyvkar Town Court held in its judgment of 5 April 2016 that restriction of access to the entire VKontakte account rather than to the specific post had a basis in law, which in substance provides for restriction of access to an entire account, taking into consideration the nature of real-time distribution of publicly accessible content on the Internet.
